newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Tourism body vows no haven for sex tourists.
newsitem.headline: Tourism body vows no haven for sex tourists.

text.p: Tourism leaders from 60 countries launched an international campaign on Thursday to combat child prostitution flourishing in major Asian destinations and vowed there would be no safe haven anywhere for sex tourists.
Delegates to the World Tourism Organisation meeting in Manila adopted a declaration urging governments to enact laws to fight drug addiction, prostitution and child abuse.

"We commit ourselves to encourage governments to promulgate and enforce legal regimes...to eliminate the undesirable social consequences of tourism through agreements that deprive malefactors of any safe haven anywhere," the Manila Declaration said.

Delegates vowed to mobilise international support and strengthen monitoring systems with the aid of governments and the private sector "with a view to promoting the positive aspects and eradicating the negative impacts of tourism", it said.

"Our message to the world is we are on an all-out war against this type of social problem," Philippine Tourism Secretary Mina Gabor told reporters at the start of the two-day meeting of tourism ministers.
Gabor said members of the organisation vowed to open extradition talks as part of their campaign against paedophiles.

"In the past 20 years, an increasing number of foreign tourists and paedophiles are travelling to Asia and other regions of the world to have sex with children," said Ron O'Grady, chairman of a Thai-based organisation against child prostitution, pornography and trafficking.
O'Grady said at least one million children under 16 years old worked as prostitutes in Asia. He said sex tourists went to countries where there were less risks of getting caught.
There are about 100,000 child prostitutes in the Philippines alone, officials said.
Gabor said the Philippines planned to hold extradition talks with Spain, Guam, Portugal, Romania and Japan on Friday.
"We will talk about extradition treaties so that if they (paedophiles) escape us, we can still continue to get hold of them by putting on them the full force of the law on the other side," she said.

The Philippines is also looking at adopting the Australian tourism federation's code of ethic which aims to screen out travel services to individuals or institutions looking for child prostitutes, Gabor said.
She said the body was planning to tap the Internet to promote the campaign.
Tourism leaders said rapid growth in the tourist industry worldwide had spawned prostitution and sex tours.
